evidence.quote: The center area was used as a horse stable; around the outside of the rock wall, there is a covered circular track that was used to exercise horses during winter months.

evidence.claim: Peter French had the barn built in the late 1870s or early 1880s. It is the only surviving round barn of the group once in the vicinity.
evidence.quote: This round barn was constructed sometime in the late 1870s or early 1880s. There were originally two—or possibly three—in the vicinity, but this is the only round barn remaining.

evidence.claim: The barn measures 100 feet across; the stone corral at its center is 60 feet in diameter.
evidence.quote: The barn is 100 feet in diameter featuring a 60-foot round stone corral

evidence.claim: Local rock and mud form the circular wall, while lumber came from 60 miles to the north.
evidence.quote: The interior of the barn consists of a circular rock wall, constructed with local rock and mud, which encloses the central stable area.  The remainder of the structure is constructed from lumber that was hauled to the site from 60 miles (97 km) to the north.

evidence.claim: Juniper posts support the interior.

evidence.claim: Diamond Craters began with molten basalt spreading in a thin layer across a dry lake bed.
evidence.quote: The craters were formed when molten basalt spilled from fissures in the earth and flooded in a thin layer over a dry lake bed.

evidence.claim: Before that layer cooled completely, more magma pushed underneath and raised six domes.
evidence.quote: Before the initial layer cooled completely, more basaltic magma injected underneath, creating six arching structural domes.

evidence.claim: In the 1970s, commercial stonecutters illegally removed lava slabs to sell as veneer for fireplaces, houses and chimneys.
evidence.quote: In the 1970s, Diamond Craters was a source of controversy between the Bureau of Land Management and commercial stonecutters who were illegally removing slabs of lava to sell as veneer for fireplaces, home exteriors, and chimneys.

evidence.claim: Geologists objected that slab harvesting and heavy equipment threatened the volcanic field’s research value.
evidence.quote: Geologists familiar with the area cited the craters' unusual research value, a "museum of basaltic volcanic features" apt to be destroyed by slab harvesting and associated heavy equipment.
